question: What is the difference between declaration and definition?

scenes.sub: A declaration introduces a name. A definition creates the thing.
scenes.say: Declaration versus definition. It sounds like word play, but it explains headers, linker errors, and the one definition rule.

scenes.head: Same names, two kinds of statements

panels.code:
extern int count;          // declaration
int add(int a, int b);     // declaration
struct Point;              // declaration

int count = 0;             // definition: memory reserved
int add(int a, int b) {    // definition: the body
    return a + b;
}
struct Point { int x, y; };  // definition: full layout

scenes.say: A declaration introduces a name and its type to the compiler. It says: this exists somewhere, trust me. A definition actually creates it. For a variable, memory is reserved. For a function, the body is written. For a class, its full layout becomes known. Every definition is also a declaration, but not the other way around.

scenes.head: This is why headers exist

items.sub: connects every call to the definition

scenes.say: The header holds only the declaration, so any file can include it, and any file can call add. Exactly one c p p file holds the definition. The compiler checks each file separately, using just the declaration, and the linker connects every call to the single definition.

scenes.head: Rule: declare many times, define once
scenes.say: The rule: you can declare something as many times as you like, but define it exactly once. This is the one definition rule. Define the same global in two files, and the linker complains about multiple definitions. The fix is to write extern int counter in a header, and define it in just one file.

scenes.head: The opposite mistake
scenes.say: The opposite mistake: declared and called, but never defined. The compiler is happy, because the declaration is enough to check the call. The linker is not, and reports an undefined reference.

lines: Declaration: introduces a name and its type. “It exists somewhere.”
Definition: creates it. Memory, a function body, or a full class layout.
Declare as often as you want. Define exactly once (ODR).
scenes.say: In one line each. A declaration introduces a name and type. A definition creates the thing: memory, a body, or a layout. Declare as often as you want, but define exactly once.
